title: Three months in: how the EU AI Act's general-purpose AI enforcement is actually working
subtitle: GPAI provisions became enforceable on August 2 with fines up to €15M or 3% of global revenue. The AI Office's first 90 days of requests and investigations give a usable picture of the new regime.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The EU AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations have been legally binding since August 2, 2025, but enforcement went live exactly a year later: on August 2, 2026, the European Commission's AI Office, working with national authorities, gained the power to investigate providers of GPAI models, order corrective measures, and impose fines up to €15 million or 3 percent of worldwide annual turnover — whichever is greater. Three months into that enforcement window, the shape of the regime is becoming clearer.

The AI Office's first public actions have been structured requests for information to the major GPAI providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Meta, and others — covering training-data provenance, copyright policies, systemic-risk assessments, and incident reporting. None of these early requests have escalated to a formal investigation or a fine, but their published templates have forced the industry to document practices many providers had previously kept internal. The December 2, 2026 deadline for a separate set of prohibitions on non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material remains on the books, though some high-risk Annex III deadlines were pushed from 2026 to 2027 in a delayed-implementation package.

The practical mechanics matter. Fines scale with global revenue, not EU revenue — so a US-based lab that serves EU customers through an API is in scope, even if its EU business is a small share of the total. Model providers are responsible for the systemic-risk work, but deployers of high-risk systems carry their own distinct set of obligations that national authorities, not Brussels, enforce. This two-track structure is where most compliance budgets are quietly being spent.

A takeaway for learners: Europe's AI regime is not primarily about fining the biggest labs. It is about forcing the entire supply chain to document what it does and why. If you plan to build on top of an open-weights model, or to deploy a vendor's API in a healthcare or hiring product, learn the provider–deployer distinction now — that is where your own legal obligations live, long before the AI Office knocks on anyone's door.
